The Fall

Welcome back. Last time the loop broke underneath her — prices fell, the payment jumped, and her family stopped paying. Today we follow her down the road that follows, step by step, in order, with nothing skipped.

Class 3 · The Fall
Our house: the 1972 house
Slide 1 of 12
Chapter 1 · From memory

Draw the loop. Now put a cross where it breaks.

No notes. Before anything new, the class rebuilds last time's loop from memory alone — jobs, pay, rates, building, prices going round — and marks the exact place it snapped for her family. That cross is where today's story starts.

If they can draw it cold, they own it. If they can't, today has nothing to stand on — so take the five minutes and find out.

Say her name first

She was named once, in Class 1. If the room needs to hear it out loud to bring her back, here it is — pick the name the class chose, or type it in.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, third chapter.
Say it in class

“Close your notes. Draw the loop from memory — jobs, pay, rates, building, prices. Now put a cross where it breaks. That cross is where today's story starts.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

People have jobs, so they earn pay. Pay lets them make the monthly house payment. The interest rate decides how much house that same payment can carry. When many people can buy, prices rise and builders build — which creates more jobs, and round it goes. It breaks where two things hit at once: the house's price falls, and the payment jumps. That's the cross.

How to run it, step by step

  1. Two minutes, silent, drawing from memory. No peeking at Class 2.
  2. Ask three people to name one link each. Fill gaps with questions, not a lecture.
  3. Ask where the cross goes — and accept more than one answer, if the reason holds.
  4. End on her: “Her family is standing on that cross right now.”

If you've done this work before

You know the cross is not academic. On a real file, the break is usually visible in the dates: a job loss, a rate reset, a value that dropped below the loan. Reading a file that way — which link snapped, and when — is the habit this drawing is really teaching.

The line to remember: “The house did not break. The loop broke.”

The proof behind it

The loop and its break are Class 2's whole lesson, sourced there: the two peaks (2,379,000 total in 1972; 1,716,000 single-family in 2005), the 2009 trough of 554,000 starts, and the rate anchors (18.63% in October 1981, 2.65% in January 2021). This class leans on that record rather than re-proving it — today starts where it ended.

If this is all new to you

Most people think it goes: miss a payment, lose the house. It doesn't. Between those two moments sits a long road — help that must be tried first, a legal process that runs differently in different states, a public sale, and only then a new owner. Today you learn the road in order, because later your work will depend on knowing exactly which step a house has reached.

The road, in order

  1. The payment stops — default.
  2. Help is tried first — loss mitigation.
  3. The legal process — foreclosure, by state law.
  4. The public sale — the auction, and the lender's credit bid.
  5. A new name — REO, or an agency home.
  6. Empty — and what emptiness does to her, week by week.

If you've done this work before

The order is the job. A processor who confuses default with foreclosure, or a filing with a repossession, will misread every status that crosses their desk. This class is deliberately slow for exactly that reason.

The line to remember: “Default is the first page of a long road — not the last.”

The proof behind it

Each step gets its own slide and its own sourcing as we reach it — the 120-day floor, the state split, the credit bid, and the 2010 numbers all arrive with their labels on. Nothing on this opening slide needs proving yet; it's a map, not a claim.

Chapter 2 · Default

The payment stops. The family still lives there.

One month the payment doesn't go. Then another. Maybe the job went. Maybe the payment grew too big. Maybe the house fell in value and the whole plan fell with it. The reason is different every time. The word for where she stands now is default — the borrower has fallen behind on the loan. And that is all it means, so far.

Her lights are still on. Her lawn is still cut. Nothing has been taken from anyone yet.

Say it in class

“Default is not the end of the story. It is the first page of a long road. If you call it the end, you will get every step after it wrong.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Think of a promise paid monthly. Default is simply: the payments have fallen behind. The family still holds the keys, still cooks in her kitchen, still owns the house in every way that matters today. The loan is in trouble. The house has not changed hands. Keep those two ideas apart and the rest of the road will make sense.

How it usually happens, step by step

  1. The loop breaks — income drops, or the payment rises, or the value falls below the loan.
  2. One payment is missed. Then a second.
  3. The loan is now in default, and letters start arriving.
  4. But the family still lives there — and the next step is help, not removal.

If you've done this work before

In the field, this distinction protects people. A house in default can look completely normal from the street — occupied, maintained, lived in — because it is. Anyone who treats “behind on payments” as “vacant” will make the most serious mistake this industry has.

The line to remember: “Behind is not gone.”

The proof behind it

This is a definition, and the class programme states it plainly: default means the borrower has fallen behind on the loan; it does not mean the house is taken. The steps that can eventually lead to a taking — and the help that must come first — are the next two chapters, each with its own rules attached.

If this is all new to you

Picture three different families in the same street. One lost a job. One kept the job, but their loan's payment jumped when the rate changed. One could still pay, but the house is now worth less than the loan — so the plan they were sold no longer adds up. Three stories, one result: the payment stops.

The three breaks, side by side

  1. Income break — the wage goes away or shrinks.
  2. Payment shock — the monthly amount rises past what the wage can carry.
  3. Value break — prices fall, the loan is bigger than the house, and there's no clean way out by selling.

Class 2's formula covers all three: price fall plus payment shock leads to default.

If you've done this work before

The reason matters for the help that follows — a temporary income break is a different conversation from a loan that can never be carried — but it never changes the order of the road. Whatever the reason, the next step is the same: loss mitigation first.

The line to remember: “The reason is different every time. The road is the same.”

The proof behind it

The programme teaches the break exactly this way — the job goes, the payment grows too big, or the price falls and the plan falls apart — as the typical causes carried from Class 2. They are taught as patterns, not statistics; no percentages are claimed for them on this page.

Chapter 3 · Loss mitigation

Help comes before punishment.

Before anyone is allowed to take the house, the loan company has to try to keep the family in it. There's a name for that trying: loss mitigation — making the loss smaller. Instead of both sides losing everything, they look for a way that hurts less. Only if those paths fail, or the family doesn't take them, does the road move on.

And there's a floor under the whole thing: as a federal rule, foreclosure generally cannot start until the loan is more than 120 days behind — about four months.

Say it in class

“Help comes before punishment. If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember the order: loss mitigation first, foreclosure second. Anyone who jumps the order is already wrong.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Taking a house is slow, expensive, and usually loses money — the house sells for less, after months of cost. So the loan company would often rather fix the loan than take the house. That's loss mitigation: both sides give a little, so neither loses everything. The family keeps a home; the lender keeps a paying loan.

How it happens, step by step

  1. The loan falls into default.
  2. The servicer — the company that manages the loan day to day — reviews the family's situation.
  3. One of the four options on the next slide is offered, if the family qualifies.
  4. If an option works, the road ends here. The house is never taken.
  5. Only if nothing works does the road move toward foreclosure.

If you've done this work before

This is why so many filings never become repossessions — a number trap you'll meet in Chapter 8. The road has exits, and a large share of families take one. Anyone forecasting “this house will be empty by spring” from a default notice alone hasn't understood this chapter.

The line to remember: “The road has exits. Many people take them.”

The proof behind it

The programme states the order as a rule of the road — loss mitigation comes before foreclosure — and names its four options, which the next slide teaches one by one. The gap between filings and actual repossessions in 2010 (about 2.9 million filings; a monthly repossession peak of 102,134) is the visible evidence that most cases leave the road before the end.

If this is all new to you

Delinquent is the plain word for behind on payments. The federal floor says foreclosure generally cannot begin until a loan is more than 120 days delinquent. In ordinary language: roughly four missed months stand between a family and the start of any legal taking — four months in which help is supposed to be tried.

Count it out

  1. Day 1–30: first payment missed. Default begins.
  2. Days 31–90: more payments missed; the loss-mitigation review is where the action is.
  3. Day 120 passes: only now can foreclosure generally start — and only if the help paths have failed.

If you've done this work before

One honest caution, and say it if the class asks: rules change. The programme itself flags this floor with “check the current text before teaching it as today's rule.” Teach the structure — a protected window for help, measured in days behind — and verify the current wording before relying on it for any real file.

The line to remember: “Four months of floor before the road can move.”

The proof behind it

As carried in the programme's verified schedule: a federal rule that foreclosure generally cannot start until the loan is more than 120 days delinquent, flagged there for re-checking against the current text before it is taught as current law. It is presented here the same way — as the floor in the story, with that caution attached.

Chapter 4 · The four options

Four doors. Know all four by name.

Loss mitigation isn't one thing — it's four different doors, and a trainee who can only name one of them doesn't know the chapter. Two of them keep the family in the house. Two of them let the family leave without a foreclosure on the record. All four beat the road ahead.

ForbearanceThe payments pause, or shrink, for a while.
·
ModificationThe loan itself changes — new terms.
·
Short saleSold for less than owed — with the lender's agreement.
·
Deed-in-lieuThe deed is handed back instead of foreclosure.
Say it in class

“Forbearance pauses it. Modification rewrites it. A short sale sells it short, with permission. A deed-in-lieu hands the paper back. Four doors — say them back to me.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Forbearance is breathing room. The payments pause, or get smaller, for a while. The loan doesn't go away — it waits. That's the right door when the break is temporary: a job lost, then found again. Modification goes further: the loan itself is rewritten. New terms. Maybe a smaller payment. Maybe more time to pay. The deal changes so the family can actually keep it.

Tell them apart

  1. Forbearance: same loan, paused or reduced payments, for a set while.
  2. Modification: a changed loan — different terms from here on.
  3. Test question: “Did the deal change, or did it just wait?” Waited = forbearance. Changed = modification.

If you've done this work before

The practical difference shows up in files: a forbearance has an end date and a catch-up question waiting behind it, while a modification settles the loan onto new terms. Confuse the two in a status note and everyone downstream plans around the wrong future.

The line to remember: “One waits. One rewrites.”

The proof behind it

Both definitions are the programme's own, word for word in substance: forbearance — payments pause or shrink for a while, the loan waits; modification — the loan itself changes, with new terms that may lower the payment or stretch the time. No figures are attached to either on this page, because none are needed to know them.

If this is all new to you

Sometimes the honest answer is that the family can't stay. A short sale sells the house for less than what's still owed — “short,” because the money comes up short — and the lender agrees to accept that smaller amount. It only happens with the lender's agreement; nobody does it alone. A deed-in-lieu skips the sale: the deed is the paper that says who owns the house, and the family hands that paper straight back to the lender. “In lieu” means instead of — instead of foreclosure.

Tell them apart

  1. Short sale: the house is sold to a buyer, for less than owed, with the lender's agreement.
  2. Deed-in-lieu: no buyer, no sale — the ownership paper goes back to the lender.
  3. Both need the lender's agreement. Neither is something a family can just do.

If you've done this work before

Why it matters on the ground: a house that leaves through one of these doors usually arrives at vacancy in better shape, on a known date, with the family gone by agreement — a completely different starting condition from a house taken through the full legal road. The door a house left by is part of its file, and part of what you'll find inside.

The line to remember: “Short means the money comes up short. In lieu means instead of.”

The proof behind it

Again the programme's definitions, taught exactly as written there: short sale — sold for less than owed, lender agrees to accept the smaller amount; deed-in-lieu — the deed handed back to the lender instead of going through foreclosure. If the class remembers the word-parts (“short,” “in lieu = instead of”), they'll never swap the two.

Chapter 5 · Foreclosure

There is no single American foreclosure.

If the help fails, the legal process begins — and here the road splits. Foreclosure is the legal process of taking the house because the loan wasn't paid, and it is state law. Each state runs it its own way. Same destination. Different road. A trainee must know which road their state uses before judging anything about a house.

Say it in class

“Say it with me, slowly: default, loss mitigation, foreclosure, auction, REO or agency home. That is the road. If you mix up the order, you mix up the house.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

In some states the road goes through a court: the lender files a lawsuit, a judge is involved, and at the end there's a sheriff sale — the sheriff is the county officer who runs the sale. In other states there's no court at all. That's called a non-judicial sale — non-judicial just means no judge. A trustee runs it instead: the person trusted to handle the sale outside court.

Side by side

Through a courtOutside a court
NameJudicial foreclosureNon-judicial sale
Who's involvedA judge, on a lender's lawsuitNo judge
Who runs the saleThe sheriffA trustee
DestinationThe same: a public auction of the house

If you've done this work before

The road changes the timing, the paperwork, and the names on the documents — which is why a timeline learned in one state is a wrong answer in another. On any real file, the first question is never “how long does foreclosure take?” It's “which state, and which road?”

The line to remember: “Same destination, different road — and the state picks the road.”

The proof behind it

Taught exactly as the programme states it: foreclosure is state law; some states go through a court (lawsuit, judge, sheriff sale), others use a non-judicial trustee sale. This page deliberately names no state as an example of either road — assignments of states to roads change and must be checked, not memorised from a demo page.

If this is all new to you

Hold her position clearly: the family has defaulted. Help was tried and didn't hold. A legal process has started in her state — whichever road that state uses. But no sale has happened yet. Until the auction, she is still the family's house in the eyes of the outcome, however heavy the paperwork has become.

The road so far

  1. Default — payments fell behind. ✔
  2. Loss mitigation — tried first, failed or not taken. ✔
  3. 120-day floor — passed. ✔
  4. Foreclosure — started, by her state's road. ← she is here
  5. Next: the auction.

If you've done this work before

“In foreclosure” is a status, not an outcome — files sit in it for a long time, and cases can still end in a sale, a cure, or a dismissal before any auction. Precision here is what keeps a status report honest.

The line to remember: “In foreclosure is a place on the road, not the end of it.”

The proof behind it

The order itself is the claim on this slide, and it is the programme's spine for the whole session: default → loss mitigation → foreclosure → auction → REO or agency home. The two mistakes the programme warns about both live here — putting the auction before foreclosure, and REO before the auction — and the road-cards exercise at the end of the class tests exactly this.

Chapter 6 · The auction

The auction. And the bid that isn't cash.

At the end of foreclosure comes a public sale: buyers bid, and the highest bid wins. But there's one bidder unlike the others. The lender is allowed to bid too — and the lender bids what it is owed. That bid is called a credit bid, because the lender is bidding credit: money it is already owed, not new cash out of its pocket.

If no buyer bids more than the lender's credit bid, the lender keeps the house. Nobody outbid the debt — so the debt keeps the house.

Say it in class

“A credit bid is the debt bidding for itself. Beat the debt, and the house is yours. Fail to beat it, and the house goes home with the lender.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Say the lender is owed 100 — an invented round number, used only to show the idea. A buyer at the auction must bid cash: real money, paid now. The lender can bid its 100 without handing over a single note, because the “money” is the debt itself. A buyer who bids 101 wins the house. Bids of 90, or no bids at all, lose to the debt.

How the sale plays out

  1. The house is offered publicly.
  2. Cash buyers bid what the house is worth to them.
  3. The lender bids up to what it is owed — the credit bid.
  4. Highest bid wins. If that's a buyer, the house is sold. If that's the lender, the lender keeps it — and the next chapter begins.

If you've done this work before

This is why so many auctioned houses end up bank-owned without anyone “choosing” that outcome: in a fallen market, the debt is often simply bigger than any cash bid in the room. The lender doesn't win the house. It fails to lose it.

The line to remember: “Nobody outbid the debt, so the debt keeps the house.”

The proof behind it

The mechanism is the programme's, stated exactly: at auction the highest bid wins; the lender may bid what it is owed — a credit bid, bidding credit rather than new cash — and if no buyer tops it, the lender keeps the house. The “100” above is a teaching number invented on this page and labelled as such; no real loan figure is used anywhere in this class.

If this is all new to you

The gavel falls and ownership changes — on paper. Inside her walls, nothing has moved. The same rooms, the same roof, the same family belongings perhaps still there. The auction settles a legal question — whose house is this now? The physical question — what state is she in? — is a different chapter, and it's coming.

Two outcomes only

  1. A buyer tops the credit bid — the house is sold at auction, and her story leaves this road.
  2. Nobody tops it — the lender keeps her, and she takes a new name in the next chapter.

If you've done this work before

Keeping “who owns it” and “what condition it's in” as separate facts is a daily discipline in this work. Files blur them constantly — an ownership date gets read as a vacancy date, a sale date as a condition report. This slide exists to keep them apart.

The line to remember: “The auction changes her owner. It doesn't touch her walls.”

The proof behind it

Nothing numerical to prove here — the claim is the road's own logic, as the programme lays it out: the auction follows foreclosure, the credit bid decides it, and the house's next name (next chapter) depends on who holds her when the bidding stops.

Chapter 7 · REO or agency home

She gets a new name. Which one depends on her loan.

The lender kept her. Now the industry stops calling her a home and starts calling her an asset — and the name tells you who holds her. If the lender keeps her, she is REO: real estate owned — bank-owned, in plain words. But if her loan was a government-insured loan, she doesn't stay with the lender. She is conveyed — handed over — to the agency that insured the loan, and becomes an agency home, sold as-is.

As-is means exactly as she stands, with no repairs promised. It is not a trick. It is the deal, stated plainly.

Say it in class

“REO means the bank owns her. An agency home means the insuring agency took her. Same empty house — two different owners, two different names. Never blur them.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Banks are in the money business, not the house business — but a credit bid can leave one holding a house anyway. The industry needed a shelf to put those houses on, and the shelf is labelled REO: Real Estate Owned. When you hear “an REO property,” translate it instantly: a house the lender ended up owning after the auction.

How a house becomes REO

  1. Default, help tried, foreclosure, auction — the whole road behind her.
  2. No cash bid tops the lender's credit bid.
  3. The lender takes title — the legal ownership.
  4. From that day, she is counted as REO until she is sold.

If you've done this work before

Hold the counting discipline for Chapter 8: a house only joins the REO pile at this step — not at default, not at filing, not at foreclosure start. Half the bad numbers in this industry come from counting her too early.

The line to remember: “REO is a shelf the bank never wanted to build.”

The proof behind it

The programme's definition, exactly: if the lender keeps the house it is called REO — real estate owned, meaning bank-owned. The December 2010 combined figure in the next chapter (about 2.2 million, in-foreclosure plus REO together) only makes sense with this definition kept strict.

If this is all new to you

Some loans carry government insurance (you met the idea in Class 1: insurance is what made banks brave enough to lend). If one of those loans fails all the way down this road, the lender doesn't keep the house — it conveys it, hands it over, to the agency that insured the loan. That agency then sells it as an agency home, as-is: what you see is what you get, no repairs promised.

Which name does she get?

  1. Was her loan government-insured? If no → the lender keeps her → REO.
  2. If yes → she is conveyed to the insuring agency → agency home.
  3. Either way she is empty, and either way she will be sold. The name tells you whose shelf she sits on while she waits.

If you've done this work before

The name matters because the shelf comes with a rulebook: whose forms, whose photo rules, whose timelines. That lesson — many clients, many rulebooks, the order in front of you governs — becomes a whole session later in the programme. It starts here, with two names for one empty house.

The line to remember: “The name tells you whose shelf she's on.”

The proof behind it

As the programme states it: on a government-insured loan, the house is conveyed to the insuring agency and becomes an agency home, sold as-is — exactly as it stands, no repairs promised. And one related figure is handled with the same care in the programme: the two agency REO piles of 2010 (Fannie Mae's and Freddie Mac's) belong to the next session's system, taught there as two piles, never one number.

Chapter 8 · Read the label

Numbers that lie if you read them fast.

The fall produced enormous numbers, and almost every one of them is quoted wrong. Not because the numbers are false — because the labels get dropped. A filing is not a home. A start is not a finish. A combined number is not one pile. Read the label before you trust the number.

Say it in class

“A filing is not a home. A start is not a finish. A combined number is not one pile. Read the label on every number, or the number will lie to you.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A filing is a paper filed to start a foreclosure case — a piece of paperwork, not a house changing hands. A start is a case begun. A repossession is a house actually taken back, at the very end of the road. The numbers shrink as you walk down that list, because most cases exit the road early — families catch up, loans get modified, houses get sold.

The three counts, labelled

~2.9 millionForeclosure filings in 2010 — papers filed, not homes taken
2,139,005Foreclosure starts at their peak, in 2009 — cases begun
102,134Repossessions in the peak month, September 2010 — houses actually taken

Same crisis, three counts, three sizes. Quoting the filing count as “homes lost” overstates the taken houses many times over.

If you've done this work before

You will meet all three counts in reports, headlines, and client summaries — often with the labels quietly missing. The professional habit from Class 2 applies unchanged: before repeating any foreclosure number, ask “counted at which step of the road?” If the answer isn't in the document, the number isn't ready to repeat.

The line to remember: “Papers, beginnings, houses — never swap them.”

The proof behind it

All three figures are the programme's verified teaching numbers: about 2.9 million filings in 2010; foreclosure starts peaking at 2,139,005 in 2009; monthly repossessions peaking at 102,134 in September 2010. Sources named in the programme's appendix: ATTOM for foreclosure filings and starts, and the U.S. Census Bureau series behind the wider housing counts.

If this is all new to you

In December 2010, if you counted every house somewhere on the road — still in foreclosure, not yet taken — and added every house already repossessed and sitting as REO, you got about 2.2 million. That's a true number about two groups together. The trap is quoting it as “2.2 million bank-owned homes.” It isn't. Half the pile, roughly, wasn't the bank's yet.

How the trap works

  1. Group one: houses in foreclosure — on the road, still the family's.
  2. Group two: houses already REO — at the end of the road, the bank's.
  3. Add them: ~2.2 million (December 2010). True — as a combined figure.
  4. Drop the word “combined,” and you've doubled the bank-owned pile with houses the bank does not own yet.

If you've done this work before

This is the peaks lesson in a darker key. In Class 2, dropping “total” or “single-family” invented a record that never happened. Here, dropping “combined” invents an inventory that never existed — and inventory numbers drive real decisions about crews, coverage, and money.

The line to remember: “Combined means added together. Say it, or don't use the number.”

The proof behind it

The programme flags this figure with its strongest warning in the session: the December 2010 combined inventory of in-foreclosure plus REO was about 2.2 million, and it must never be taught as REO alone. This page carries the figure with the warning attached, exactly as sourced.

Chapter 9 · Vacancy decay — the first signals

Week one: she starts telling the street she's empty.

The family is gone. And within days, she begins to announce it. The lawn grows past neat. Mail piles up in the box, then against the door. Nothing dramatic — and that is exactly the point. An overgrown lawn and a stuffed mailbox are a signal anyone walking past can read: nobody lives here. The house starts telling the street she is empty, and the street listens.

Say it in class

“Vacancy itself is damage. Nobody has to hit the house for the house to break. Empty is enough.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A lived-in house maintains itself quietly, a hundred small acts a week: the lawn cut, the mail brought in, a curtain moved, a light changed. Remove the people and the acts stop all at once. The first two stops anyone can see from the pavement are the grass and the mail. They are small. They are also a broadcast.

Week one, as the street sees it

  1. The lawn misses its cut — then another. It starts to look different from every other lawn on the street.
  2. Mail and flyers gather, uncollected, day after day.
  3. Neighbours notice. Then strangers notice.
  4. Everything in the next two chapters walks through the door this signal opens.

If you've done this work before

You already know these two signals by their work names: the overgrown lot is why grass cuts exist, and the piled mail is one of the first occupancy signs an inspector reads. This chapter is the “why” underneath routines that can otherwise look like mere tidiness.

The line to remember: “The lawn and the mailbox speak first.”

The proof behind it

The programme teaches this week-by-week decay explicitly as a teaching illustration — a typical pattern, not a research-sourced timeline — and this page says so on the slide itself, in the open. The claim being taught is the pattern and its logic, not a promise about any individual house's calendar.

If this is all new to you

A seal is the strip or edge that keeps wind and rain out of a door or window. Seals age and crack in lived-in houses too — but there, somebody notices the draught, sees the drip, wipes it up, makes a call. In an empty house, a small leak or a broken seal lets water in, and the weather works on the house day and night, unopposed. Water does what water does when nobody stops it: it spreads.

How small becomes serious

  1. A seal fails, or a small leak starts — an ordinary, fixable fault.
  2. Rain finds the way in. Nobody mops it, dries it, or reports it.
  3. Damp sits in wood, plaster, and carpet, week after week.
  4. By the end of the month, the “small fault” is a damaged room — and it's still raining.

If you've done this work before

Every experienced eye in this work reads water first, because water is the damage that keeps charging rent while a house waits. The lesson under the routine: the interval between visits is not dead time. It's the time damage uses.

The line to remember: “Water does what water does when nobody stops it.”

The proof behind it

Same honest footing as the whole decay sequence: the programme presents weeks 2–4 — a small leak or broken seal letting water in, weather working on the house — as its teaching sketch of a typical empty house. The definitions (a seal keeps wind and rain out) are the programme's own.

Chapter 10 · Vacancy decay — damp becomes damage

Month two: damp becomes mold. Small becomes big.

Still air and standing damp are an invitation, and mold accepts it — the dark, spotty growth that loves damp, still places. A stain becomes a soft floor. A soft floor becomes a room you cannot trust to walk in. Nothing dramatic happened to her. That's the whole tragedy of this chapter: small, ignored, becomes big, expensive.

Say it in class

“A stain becomes a soft floor. A soft floor becomes a room you can't trust. She didn't need a storm. She needed somebody to show up — and nobody did.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Mold doesn't arrive from nowhere. It grows where damp sits undisturbed — and an empty house is damp and undisturbed by definition. First the smell and the spots. Then the damage underneath: plaster softening, wood swelling, floors losing their strength. By the time mold is easy to see, the water that feeds it has usually been at work for weeks.

The chain, link by link

  1. Water gets in (last chapter's leak or seal).
  2. Damp stays — no heating, no air moving, no one drying it.
  3. Mold grows on the damp surfaces.
  4. Materials soften and weaken — the stain is now a structural worry.
  5. The fix is no longer a wipe and a fan. It's a repair bill.

If you've done this work before

The later sessions will teach damage reading properly — water, mold, vandalism, weather, neglect, each with its signs. This chapter plants the ordering instinct those sessions rely on: find the moisture first. Paint over mold without stopping the water and you've decorated a problem, not fixed one.

The line to remember: “Mold is a symptom. Water is the disease.”

The proof behind it

The sequence — month two, damp becomes mold, small damage becomes big damage — is the programme's teaching sketch, labelled as such on Slide 9 and here. The definitions are the programme's: mold is the dark, spotty growth that loves damp, still air. No timeline is promised for any individual house.

If this is all new to you

Median means the middle: half of homes older, half younger. In 2024 the middle owner-occupied home — a home people own and live in — was 42 years old. Our house, born in 1972, is past fifty by then. She doesn't fall empty as a young house with one small problem. She falls empty as an old house, with layers of them, and old seals, old pipes, and old roofs decay faster than new ones.

The age of the stock, in three numbers

42 yearsMedian age of an owner-occupied home, 2024
31 yearsThe same median, back in 2005 — the stock is aging
~47%Of owner-occupied homes were built before 1980

If you've done this work before

Age is a working fact, not background colour: it predicts the systems you'll find, the failures you'll meet, and why two houses on the same street, emptied the same month, can be in utterly different shape a season later. Read the year before you read the damage.

The line to remember: “Older houses, older problems — in layers.”

The proof behind it

The programme's figures, sourced there to the U.S. Census Bureau: median owner-occupied home age 42 in 2024, up from 31 in 2005, with about 47 percent of owner-occupied homes built before 1980. Her birth year, 1972, puts her squarely inside that older half.

Chapter 11 · Vacancy decay — people notice

Month three: vandals notice. Then the street pays.

The signal from week one has been broadcasting for months now, and the wrong audience has heard it. Vandals — people who break in to damage or strip a place — come through the door the emptiness opened. Fixtures go missing. Copper goes missing: the metal in her pipes and wires, worth stealing precisely because it's worth money. And she slides, in the word the industry uses, from lived-in to blighted — run-down, empty, and dragging the street down with her.

One blighted house pulls at its neighbours' prices, their safety, and their pride in the street. Her fall is no longer only her family's story.

Say it in class

“She slid from lived-in to blighted without a single storm. Empty did that — week by week, in the open, while the street watched.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A lived-in house defends itself just by being lived in: lights, sounds, someone who'd notice a stranger. Strip that away and what's left is a building full of saleable material with nobody watching it. Copper pipes and wiring can be sold as scrap metal. Fixtures — taps, fittings, appliances — can be carried out and sold. The theft isn't random cruelty; it's the economics of an unwatched house.

Month three onward, as it unfolds

  1. The vacancy signal (grass, mail, dark windows) has run for months.
  2. Someone tests the house — a window, a back door.
  3. Fixtures and copper are taken; each visit leaves the house more open than the last.
  4. Weather now has help getting in — last chapter's decay accelerates.

If you've done this work before

This is the chapter that explains why securing a house — locks, boards, the work of a later session — is urgent rather than administrative. Every week unsecured is a week the house is advertised to exactly the wrong readers.

The line to remember: “An empty house advertises itself. Securing it turns the sign off.”

The proof behind it

The pattern — month three onward, vandals notice, fixtures and copper go missing, the house slides toward blighted — is the closing step of the programme's teaching sketch, labelled as a typical pattern since Slide 9. The definitions are the programme's: vandals break in and damage or strip; copper is the metal in pipes and wires, worth stealing.

If this is all new to you

Blighted means run-down, empty, and dragging the street down with it. A blighted house lowers what the house next door can sell for. It makes the street feel less safe, because it is less watched. And it chips at something harder to price: the neighbours' pride in where they live. Her fall began as a private trouble — a missed payment. It ends as a public cost.

How the cost spreads

  1. Prices: buyers discount the whole street for the house nobody maintains.
  2. Safety: an unwatched house attracts the activity of the last point.
  3. Pride: people stop investing in a street that looks given up on.
  4. Which is why getting her secured, kept, and eventually sold again is work the whole street benefits from.

If you've done this work before

Say this plainly to anyone who thinks preservation is “just tidying empty houses”: the work exists because vacancy is contagious. Every secured, cut, and honestly reported house is a street that doesn't slide. That's the public case for the whole industry, in one chapter.

The line to remember: “Vacancy is contagious. So is care.”

The proof behind it

The definition and the spread — prices, safety, and pride in the street — are the programme's own closing words for the decay sequence: one blighted house pulls at its neighbours' prices, safety, and pride in the street. It is taught as the meaning of blight, not as a priced statistic, and no figure is attached to it here.

Chapter 12 · The road cards, and the close

Put the road in order. Then defend one step out loud.

Pairs work. Below are the road's steps, shuffled. Put them back in order — from the missed payment to the vacant house — by tapping them in the order they happen. Then pick one placement and defend it out loud: why does this card sit here, and not one step earlier or later? Reasoning is what's graded here. Guessing is the only wrong answer that matters.

The road cards

Tap the cards in the order the road runs. A card that doesn't belong next will be sent back — try the step that truly comes next. The two classic mix-ups to watch for: the auction does not come before the foreclosure that allows it, and she is not REO before anyone has bid.

Your road, in order: nothing placed yet.
Six cards. One road. Begin with the step where her story today began.

Nobody is paid to care about her — yet. Who steps in? That is next session, where the class meets the system: the nationals, the proof, and the rules.

Say it in class — the close

“There is one road and it has one order. Put it in order, and tell me why. If you can defend the order, you understand the fall.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A strong defence sounds like this: “Foreclosure sits after loss mitigation, because help must be tried before the house can be taken.” Notice the shape — a placement, then the word “because,” then the reason the order can't be swapped. Any card defended in that shape is a pass, even while another card somewhere is still out of place.

What the teacher listens for

  1. The cards end in the correct order.
  2. One placement is defended with a “because.”
  3. No step is skipped — all six cards on the road.
  4. Correct the order, not the person, when a pair slips — and praise good reasoning out loud when you hear it.

If you've done this work before

The quick check, if time runs short: “Put these three in order — auction, loss mitigation, foreclosure.” Thirty seconds, and you know exactly who has the road and who has a blur. The blur is fixable tonight; it is expensive on a live file.

The line to remember: “If you can defend the order, you understand the fall.”

The proof behind it

The exercise, its two classic mistakes, its rubric, and its model sentence are all the programme's own decision moment for this session, carried over whole. The road it tests is the same order every chapter of this page followed — nothing new is introduced at the test.

If this is all new to you

If you keep nothing else: the road in order — default, loss mitigation, foreclosure, auction, REO or agency home, vacant house. The four loss-mitigation doors by name. The three label-rules — a filing is not a home, a start is not a finish, a combined number is not one pile. And the sentence: vacancy itself is damage. That's the whole class in one pocket.

Her whole fall, step by step

  1. The loop broke; the payment stopped — default, lights still on.
  2. Help was tried first — four doors, and a 120-day floor under them.
  3. It failed. Foreclosure ran her state's road — court or trustee.
  4. At auction, nobody outbid the debt. The credit bid kept her.
  5. She took a new name — REO, or an agency home sold as-is.
  6. Empty, she decayed: signal, water, mold, stripping, blight.

If you've done this work before

Next session changes the scale: from one house's road to the system built to walk thousands of houses down it — the nationals who organise the work, the proof that learned to travel faster, and the rules that say permission first, proof always. This road is that system's reason for existing. Bring it with you, in order, from memory.

The line to remember: “Nobody is paid to care about her — yet.”

The proof — the whole fall, in one place

The floorForeclosure generally cannot start until a loan is more than 120 days delinquent (federal rule — check the current text before teaching it as today's rule).
2009Foreclosure starts peak: 2,139,005 cases begun.
2010About 2.9 million filings in the year; repossessions peak at 102,134 in September — this page's passcode year.
Dec 2010Combined in-foreclosure + REO inventory about 2.2 million — combined, never REO alone.
2024Median owner-occupied home: 42 years old; about 47% built before 1980.

Sources, as named in the programme's appendix: ATTOM (filings and starts), the U.S. Census Bureau (home age and pre-1980 share). The week-by-week decay remains what it was labelled on its own slide: a teaching sketch of a typical pattern, not a sourced timeline.

Tip: use the ← and → keys to move between chapters — and open the full notes on any slide to re-learn the topic from scratch

All 12 slides

The full arc of Class 3 on one screen — the loop redrawn, the payment stopped, help tried first, the legal road, the auction, her new name, the numbers with their labels on, and what emptiness does to her week by week. Tap any slide to jump to it.

The logic behind this page

Why Class 3 is built as one road in one order, why its numbers are taught as labels, and where its one honest sketch is labelled as a sketch. One teacher to another, before the class walks in.

A road, not a pile of topics

The session's spine is sequence. Default, loss mitigation, foreclosure, auction, REO or agency home, vacant house — each step only makes sense standing on the one before it, and the two errors the programme warns about (auction before foreclosure; REO before the auction) are both errors of order, not of knowledge. So the page teaches nothing out of order, and its closing exercise tests nothing but order, defended out loud. A trainee who leaves with the order owns the session; a trainee who leaves with facts but a shuffled road has a blur that will cost money on a real file.

Help before punishment is a rule, not a mood

  • The order is legal, not sentimental. Loss mitigation must be tried before foreclosure, and a federal floor generally bars a foreclosure start until a loan is more than 120 days delinquent. The page teaches both — and carries the programme's own caution that the floor's current text should be checked before it is taught as today's rule.
  • The four doors are taught by name because “loss mitigation” as a blur helps no one: forbearance (the loan waits), modification (the loan changes), short sale (sold short, with the lender's agreement), deed-in-lieu (the paper handed back, instead of foreclosure). Each is defined by the word-part a trainee can carry.

Why the numbers chapter sits in the middle

  • It is the peaks lesson, applied where it bites. Class 2 taught “read the label” on friendly building counts. Chapter 8 replays the same discipline on crisis counts — filings (~2.9M, 2010), starts (2,139,005 peak, 2009), monthly repossessions (102,134, September 2010), and the combined inventory (~2.2M, December 2010, never REO alone) — where dropping a label doesn't just misremember history, it invents inventory.
  • The shrinkage is the story. Filings to starts to repossessions falls by design: the road has exits, and Chapter 3's help is where most cases leave. The numbers chapter quietly proves the loss-mitigation chapter.

The one sketch, labelled as a sketch

  • The week-by-week vacancy decay (week 1 signal; weeks 2–4 water and weather; month 2 mold; month 3 onward vandalism, copper, blight) is the programme's teaching illustration of a typical pattern — not a research-sourced timeline. The page says so on the slide itself, in the figure caption, and again in the evidence drawers. Real houses vary.
  • Everything else on the page is either a definition (default, credit bid, REO, deed, seal, trustee), a sourced figure (Chapter 8 and the home-age numbers: median 42 in 2024, from 31 in 2005; ~47% built before 1980), or the road's own order. The worked credit-bid example uses an invented round “100” and labels it invented.
  • Foreclosure's state split is taught without assigning any state to either road — that mapping must be checked, not memorised from a demo page.

Running the class from this page

  • Open cold, again. Slide 1 redraws Class 2's loop from memory and marks the break. Do not re-teach the loop; ask the questions that lead back to it.
  • Guard the order all hour. Any trainee who jumps the road — “so the bank repossessed it when they missed a payment” — gets a warm correction on the spot: which step did we skip?
  • Protect the road cards. If time runs short, cut discussion elsewhere — never the ordering exercise on Slide 12. The cards they placed are this class's memory anchor.
  • Nothing here is real client data — the house is a teaching character, carried from Class 1; every figure is published history or labelled teaching arithmetic.

Where it all came from

Built from the programme's own blueprint for Session 3, “The Fall: From Missed Payment to Vacant House,” and its verified 10-hour schedule. In short:

  • Foreclosure filings and starts (2010 filings; 2009 starts peak): ATTOM, as named in the programme's source appendix.
  • Home age and pre-1980 share (median 42 in 2024, 31 in 2005; ~47% pre-1980): the U.S. Census Bureau, as named in the programme's source appendix.
  • The road, the four loss-mitigation options, the 120-day floor (flagged in the programme for re-checking against current text), the judicial / non-judicial split, the credit bid, REO and agency-home definitions: the programme blueprint for Session 3.
  • The vacancy-decay sequence: the programme's teaching illustration, labelled as such wherever it appears.

This is the demo version of Class 3 from the preservation training programme — shared so the teacher can look it over before the full class is built. Our house is a teaching character, made up for the story; the pictures are illustrations, not a real property. The figures are published housing and foreclosure history, the one worked example is labelled invented, and everything here is a teaching example — no real clients, work orders, or company details anywhere on the page.
